```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
skills <- read.csv("data/digital_skills_age_eu.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(skills[c("geo", "ind_type", "time")]))
value <- function(country, age, year) {
  z <- skills$values[skills$geo == country & skills$ind_type == age & skills$time == year]
  stopifnot(length(z) == 1L, !is.na(z))
  z
}
pct <- function(z) sprintf("%.1f%%", z)
pp <- function(z) sprintf("%.1f", z)
older <- subset(skills, time == 2025 & geo != "EU27_2020" & ind_type == "Y65_74")
younger <- subset(skills, time == 2025 & geo != "EU27_2020" & ind_type == "Y25_34")
pairs <- merge(older[c("geo", "values")], younger[c("geo", "values")],
               by = "geo", suffixes = c("_older", "_younger"))
stopifnot(nrow(pairs) == 27, !anyNA(pairs))
```

## A country's lead depends on whose skills we examine

Estonia leads Germany among adults aged 25–34. Among adults aged 65–74, Germany leads Estonia. **This reversal appears in every year examined: 2021, 2023 and 2025.**

In 2025, the younger group's estimates were `r pct(value("EE", "Y25_34", 2025))` in Estonia and `r pct(value("DE", "Y25_34", 2025))` in Germany. For the older group, Germany's estimate was `r pct(value("DE", "Y65_74", 2025))`, compared with Estonia's `r pct(value("EE", "Y65_74", 2025))`.

A country comparison can therefore give a different answer depending on the age group. That is the starting point for our question: **who shares in digital progress?**

![Estonia has higher estimates than Germany for ages 25–34, while Germany has higher estimates for ages 65–74 in 2021, 2023 and 2025.](images/digital_skills_reversal_years.png){#fig-reversal width=100% fig-alt="Two panels compare Estonia and Germany in 2021, 2023 and 2025. Estonia leads at ages 25–34 in all three years; Germany leads at ages 65–74."}

@fig-reversal shows that the reversal is present in all three survey years. Germany's lead among the older group was `r pp(value("DE", "Y65_74", 2021) - value("EE", "Y65_74", 2021))` percentage points in 2021, `r pp(value("DE", "Y65_74", 2023) - value("EE", "Y65_74", 2023))` in 2023 and `r pp(value("DE", "Y65_74", 2025) - value("EE", "Y65_74", 2025))` in 2025. These are descriptive differences between estimates; we have not tested statistical significance.

## Older adults have lower estimates in every EU country

The selected countries sit within a wider European pattern. In `r sum(pairs$values_older < pairs$values_younger)` of the 27 EU countries, the 2025 estimate for ages 65–74 is below that for ages 25–34.

The connecting segments in @fig-europe show the difference between these two age groups within each country. Longer segments indicate larger gaps in percentage points. They do not represent people losing skills as they age: the two dots describe different groups of people.

![Digital-skills estimates for ages 25–34 and 65–74 in all 27 EU countries in 2025, ranked by the older group's estimate.](images/digital_skills_eu_comparison.png){#fig-europe width=100% fig-alt="A horizontal paired-dot chart for 27 EU countries. Every country's estimate for ages 65–74 is lower than its estimate for ages 25–34. Countries are ordered by the older group's result, from Ireland at the top to Romania at the bottom."}

## Older adults' experiences also differ between countries

Age does not tell the whole story. Among adults aged 65–74, the estimates range from `r pct(min(older$values))` in Romania to `r pct(max(older$values))` in Ireland. The EU-27 aggregate for this age group is `r pct(value("EU27_2020", "Y65_74", 2025))`.

This variation matters: treating older adults as one uniform group would miss substantial differences between countries. Our data describe those differences, but cannot establish why they exist.

The six-group comparison in @fig-profiles adds detail. Germany's estimates are below the EU benchmark for ages 16–54 and above it for ages 55–74. Estonia shows the reverse pattern. Romania is below the benchmark in all six age groups.

![Six age-group estimates for Estonia, Germany and Romania in 2025, with the EU-27 aggregate repeated as a dashed benchmark.](images/digital_skills_age_panels.png){#fig-profiles width=100% fig-alt="Three country panels show six age groups from 16–24 to 65–74. Estonia is above the EU benchmark for the first four groups and below for the final two. Germany has the reverse pattern. Romania is below the benchmark for every group."}

## Why this matters beyond the chart

Imagine booking a medical appointment, completing a public-service form or managing banking online. A service being available online does not establish that everyone can use it independently.

Our findings encourage readers to ask a more specific question than whether a country is digitally advanced: **which groups are included in that assessment?** They also support examining the needs of different groups when designing services. The figures alone do not establish which support or policy intervention would work best.

Older adults have diverse abilities and experiences. These results should not be read as a judgement about an individual's competence based on age.

## Audience and prioritised story points

This story is for people who encounter digital services in everyday life, support relatives online, or work in community organisations and public services. No university background or statistical knowledge is assumed.

Our guiding question is: **How do digital skills differ across age groups in the EU, and how do Germany, Estonia and Romania compare with the wider European pattern?**

| Priority | Main insight | Supporting visual |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Estonia leads Germany at ages 25–34, while Germany leads at ages 65–74, in all three years examined. | @fig-reversal |
| 2 | The 65–74 estimate is below the 25–34 estimate in all 27 EU countries in 2025. | @fig-europe |
| 3 | Results among older adults vary substantially across countries; a single age-group label conceals different national contexts. | @fig-europe and @fig-profiles |

## Data and interpretation

We use [Eurostat's Individuals' level of digital skills dataset](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_sk_dskl_i21/default/table?lang=en), code `isoc_sk_dskl_i21`. The selected measure is basic or above-basic overall digital skills (`I_DSK2_BAB`), expressed as a percentage of individuals (`PC_IND`).

The saved extract contains **`r nrow(skills)` country–age–year records**, covering 27 EU countries plus the EU-27 aggregate, six age groups and three years. There are `r sum(is.na(skills$values))` missing values: Ireland, ages 16–24, in 2021. We leave this value missing. It does not enter the charts presented here.

The 2025 Europe-wide paired-dot chart uses 54 estimates. The three-country age profiles use 18 country estimates plus six EU benchmark estimates. The three-year reversal chart uses 12 estimates.

The indicator is based on reported digital activities, rather than a direct skills test. The analysis uses group-level survey estimates, not individual respondent records. People aged 75 or older are outside the selected age range. The EU benchmark is Eurostat's aggregate, not a simple average calculated from the 27 countries.

Differences across age groups are not individual ageing trajectories. Differences between survey years do not necessarily describe the same people. We do not infer causes from these descriptive comparisons or calculate confidence intervals from the supplied extract.

::: {.callout-important title="Validation still required before final submission"}
The CSV does not contain observation-quality flags. Review Eurostat's reliability flags, methodological notes and breaks in series before making final claims about cross-country or year-to-year comparability. The present figures support visual drafts, not a completed source-quality audit.
:::

### Reproduce the analysis

The following folded code reproduces the main comparison table from the saved extract.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reversal
#| tbl-cap: "Germany and Estonia: estimates and differences in percentage points. Differences use the underlying values before rounding."
comparison <- merge(
  subset(skills, geo == "DE" & ind_type %in% c("Y25_34", "Y65_74"),
         select = c(time, ind_type, values)),
  subset(skills, geo == "EE" & ind_type %in% c("Y25_34", "Y65_74"),
         select = c(time, ind_type, values)),
  by = c("time", "ind_type"), suffixes = c("_DE", "_EE")
)
comparison <- comparison[order(comparison$time, comparison$ind_type), ]
comparison$gap <- comparison$values_EE - comparison$values_DE
comparison$ind_type <- ifelse(comparison$ind_type == "Y25_34", "25–34", "65–74")
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Year", "Age group", "Germany (%)", "Estonia (%)",
                           "Estonia minus Germany (pp)"))
```

The figures are generated by [digital_skills_visuals.R](digital_skills_visuals.R) and [digital_skills_eu_comparison.R](digital_skills_eu_comparison.R). Run these from the project root using the saved CSV before rendering the report. The report embeds those exported images; it does not silently refresh the data or regenerate the figures.

| Visual | Purpose and design choice | Refinements for the final version |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Three-year comparison | Lines show the three ordered survey years. Separate age panels expose the reversal; shared scales and different point shapes support comparison. | Use a more conversational headline; complete the source-quality review; check labels at final presentation size. |
| EU paired-dot comparison | Position on a shared percentage scale compares two age groups. Countries are ordered by the older group's result. | Inspect at full resolution; prepare a focused, larger-label version for slides; consider highlighting Germany, Estonia and Romania. |
| Three-country profiles | Separate panels compare each country's six age groups with the same EU benchmark. | Consider a dot-plot alternative for direct country comparisons; check benchmark visibility and avoid implying individual ageing. |

The circular pitch visual is retained in the repository as exploratory work. The report prioritises the charts above for easier comparison.

## Conclusion

A country's digital-skills lead can reverse when we change the age group under consideration. That reversal persists across all three years in the Germany–Estonia comparison. Across the EU, older adults' estimates are consistently lower than younger adults', but older adults' results also vary widely between countries.

Digital progress therefore deserves an age-specific view. The next explanatory question is why these differences exist—a question this descriptive dataset alone cannot answer.

## Sources and further reading

- [Eurostat: Individuals' level of digital skills, dataset isoc_sk_dskl_i21](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_sk_dskl_i21/default/table?lang=en). Indicator and unit are specified above; analysis uses the saved project extract.
- [Leppiman, Riivits-Arkonsuo and Pohjola (2021), Old-Age Digital Exclusion as a Policy Challenge in Estonia and Finland](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-51406-8_32). Background reading motivating the topic; it does not establish the causes of our observed differences.
